Geomancy is the art of <term>points</term> <note>Latin: *punctorum*; in geomancy, random dots are marked in sand or paper to form divinatory figures</note> in the place of the stars of the sky and the planets.
He who wishes to learn the art of geomancy well as to the
first principle [should know] that it is a daughter of the art of astrology and is to be imitated, because Geomancy
manifestly follows astrology in its entirety and is produced by it. And so that
a learned man might be able to be [skilled] wherever he wishes, in his heart or in his mind,
by the movement of his own good business, and it was his higher intention to examine
according to the <term>constitution of a nativity</term> <note>The planetary alignment at a person's birth, used here to validate the geomantic reading</note> and to judge concerning the matter about which knowledge is to be
found; it must be known how to sufficiently grasp the truth which without doubt
appears from this to one seeing the matter, so that with the fullness of the art a man may know
all things sufficient to be shown for the present, so as to have true knowledge of the
matters being sought. First, he ought to learn and keep in mind, namely,
whether he is able to know [the thing]. And whether a man can give counsel or a right judgment,
since every question is as much a matter of counsel over doubts. And the second thing
to be known is that this art must be observed in all things with much discretion of
wit, ordered and written according to its rules, lest at various times
diligence be held through the error of some fallacy. For while error can
happen in the master, it is not in the art itself, which is not improbable or
unreasonable; it is in the truth so that it might render to man the manifest
truth concerning doubts, and it warns in defense when there is no question regarding this.
It must be known that the whole fruit of this art is to know well how to judge,
just as it often occurs to God in every place of the world where [there is]
a city of men according to right reason; for even the super-
celestial bodies move and flow uniformly, just as different craftsmen
build one house together.

It must be known concerning the points by the authority and use of the <term>Saracens</term> <note>Latin: *Sarracenorum*; refers to the Arabic practitioners who developed 'ilm al-raml' (science of the sand), the precursor to Western geomancy</note> who
observe this on account of their old law, by celebrating in this part upon
firm sand or in the dust of the earth, as in the morning; and if it is done in a house,
upon a table or upon paper in which it is written and not weakened;
and so that this may be done lawfully by itself, the daughter of such a way of knowing. The
erection or raising of the points is through this raising of the <term>four elements</term> <note>The 16 geomantic figures are built from four lines, each corresponding to one of the classical elements</note>
and I do not know how to be understood thus, for I take up the observance at the end,
brought forth since in it so many more things will have been trusted. But because the city would rejoice and
it seems to me that whoever wishes to do well for himself and seeks a thing through which [to know],
then he owes more what belongs to him or another, according to what <unclear>is fitting</unclear>
lawfully and truly in every place by itself, if the question is raised and lifted by the art.

The method of raising the art is brief and easy because it is performed through <term>points</term> <note>The foundational act of geomancy: making random marks in a medium to generate divinatory symbols.</note>. One method is by long lines, etc., in an open area or in the manner of a ditch, etc., in a certain length and pace <gloss>namely</gloss> in the earth or on paper, whether it be done in a vein <note>likely a vein of ore or a streak in the earth</note> or in polished dust such as ash, or upon a <term>waxed tablet</term> <note>original: *tabula cerata*; a common medieval writing surface that could be smoothed over and reused</note>, or an open floor, etc. Whether it be done in sand or in another material, it is sufficient for raising this art until four lines [are made], in the likeness of the four fingers <gloss>namely</gloss> of the left hand in the hollow of the palm, as in this example:

<image-desc>A diagram in red ink. On the left is a grid of sixteen horizontal red lines. To the right is a line drawing of a left hand, palm-up. Each of the four fingers is divided into three segments, with each segment containing a horizontal row of small circles (geomantic points). The index finger has segments with 6, 8, and 10 points; the middle finger has 8, 9, and 11; the ring finger has 10, 11, and 12; and the little finger has 12, 13, and 15 (approximate counts). The thumb is on the right.</image-desc>

And without that number and without that measure of the length of the lines—supposing there are not twelve lines drawn here—two points ought to be canceled or tied together <note>The process of pairing points to determine if a line is odd (one point) or even (two points).</note>, wherefore he makes a "tie" [ligature] as in the example of the part and it ends in the use of the left. And yet it must be noted that two points at the head are dismissed <gloss>ii</gloss> <note>original: *ii*; indicating the Roman numeral for two or a pair of points</note> they stand as one [when paired], yet they are left for the "raisings" of the figure for those having need in the first figures, because the natural figures [pertain to] the four <term>elements</term> <note>original: *iiii[or] eleme[n]ta*</note>, namely: fire, air, water, and earth. Afterward, other figures are extracted from them until they have sixteen, of which [the ones called] the <term>Judge</term> <note>original: *iudex*; the primary figure used to summarize the reading</note> and the <term>Finisher</term> <note>original: *finitor*; also known as the Reconciler, the final figure that concludes the chart</note> are properly named from the first. 

Or, by making lines of points by following the raising in the natural matter of such figures from which others proceed, as in the example given in which area two points at the end of the line are dismissed. <term>Diminution</term> <gloss>namely</gloss> if the lines have [none], no utility would come from the line nor would the figure respond, and thus the art could not be raised. And if one point is found at the end of the line, it has no companion with which it might be tied, and therefore it must be left loose, so that now the order of elements and the integrity of the figures may be made. And just as the lines were in the order of the four elements, so it preserves every flow. And therefore the four first figures which are gathered through the <term>sowing of points</term> <note>original: *seminac[i]one pu[n]ctor[um]*; the act of marking the surface to start the divination</note> have each sign... which are sought by those inquiring and are called the <term>Mothers</term> <note>original: *matres*; the first four figures of a geomantic chart, representing the foundation of the question</note>. Indeed, those which come out from these four which are the Mothers are called [the Daughters] <note>The text here uses abbreviations "ar. b. i." which likely refer to the *Filiae* or Daughters, the next set of figures generated in the process.</note>...

<meta>This page continues the introduction to the art of geomancy, moving from the physical method of marking points to the theoretical and historical justification for the practice, specifically contrasting it with the technical difficulties of astrology.</meta>

...as branches emerge from a tree:

**T**he reason why this art was invented is manifold, and the principal reason is the great necessity for obtaining counsel, insofar as you may know the art of astrology according to its surface and doctrine. For the art of astrology is one of the seven <term>liberal arts</term> <note>The core curriculum of medieval education, consisting of the trivium (grammar, logic, rhetoric) and the quadrivium (arithmetic, geometry, music, and astronomy/astrology).</note> through which counsel increased by truth is held, as those properly moved by men. Because man himself was in need of another [art] by necessity, because [astrology] requires its own <term>geometric instruments</term> <note>original: *instrumenta geomatalia*</note>, many books such as tables, many square tables, and other rules of judgment without which it cannot be practiced. And in addition to that, it requires more than anything else clear weather, so that from the serenity of the air by day the bright sun may be seen and its rays received through the two holes of the plates of the <term>square astrolabe instrument</term> <note>A specialized astronomical tool used for measuring the altitude of celestial bodies to determine time and position.</note>, or a fixed star at night. And thus, if these things are otherwise, counsel cannot be obtained through that art. Since the air is often turbulent or the rest of the doctrine cannot bear fruit, therefore the art of <term>geomancy</term> <note>Divination using patterns of points made in the earth or on paper.</note> was invented to be formed and counsel obtained through it at all times, by day and night, whether it be clear or cloudy, and without the impediment of any expense. Nor does it require [long] schooling nor a [specific] hour, but every time a man wishes to propose his question, he can do it, and the tree [the geomantic chart] can be raised and the truth held; the body which it carries <unclear>appearing</unclear> to be of the truth.

For geomancy is the daughter of astronomy, and is <unclear>joined</unclear> to it, and she follows it in all things through its <unclear>succession</unclear>. All things in it are wisely estimated, since in all mysteries and its own entire judgments of the <term>heavens</term> <note>original: *coili*, a variant of *caeli*</note> and of those things which now are, they come from the dispersed stars, planets, and the four elements.

<image-desc>A diagram drawn in red ink consisting of a shield-shaped frame. The interior of the shield is divided into a 4x4 grid, creating sixteen rectangular cells. Each cell contains a unique geomantic figure composed of a vertical sequence of one or two dots. These figures represent the traditional sixteen signs of geomancy.</image-desc>

**H**ec This art of geomancy had its origin from God, because Solomon says wisdom was given to Adam from Him. And John the Evangelist, when he made the beginning [of his Gospel], it was; and elsewhere it says: "I am the <term>Alpha and Omega</term> <note>The first and last letters of the Greek alphabet, used here to signify God as the beginning and end of all things.</note>, the beginning and the end of all things that are, were, and shall be." However, there is an opinion that it had its beginning through second [causes] and the spirituality of <unclear>wicked</unclear> men from certain angels who fell from heaven when the ruin was properly perpetuated above...

<summary>This page justifies geomancy as a practical alternative to astrology, noting that while astrology requires expensive tools and clear skies, geomancy is accessible at any time. It further establishes the art's legitimacy by calling it the "daughter of astronomy" and tracing its origins to divine wisdom given to Adam and Solomon.</summary>

<meta>This page continues the discussion on the origins of geomancy, moving from its practical advantages over astrology to its legendary lineage and the proper spiritual conduct required of a "querent" (the person asking the question) when approaching a master of the art.</meta>

<page-num>4.</page-num>

Here, some say that Lucifer <note>original: *lucifer*; likely referring to the "Light-Bringer" in a mythological sense or the fallen angel as a source of forbidden knowledge</note> himself taught it. Others, however, provide many different accounts, adding that it was Shem, the son of Noah, before the Flood. Others say that the son of Noah was not sufficient, for it is said that there was no prior author except God, because it was the will of God that what was spoken should come to pass; at some other time, it was explained more fully and distinctly than it ever had been before. Others say it was the Sibyl <note>A Greco-Roman prophetess; medieval traditions often retroactively attributed various occult arts to her</note>; others say it was Ptolemy, the King of Egypt. And it is also said that this art took its origin—as is publicly found—before the time of the Deluge of waters which occurred in the days of Noah, who built the Ark by the command of God.

Another inquiry regarding this matter was made: it ought to be practiced wisely. Not every person should [perform it] principally at every hour of the day or night, for the matter [ought not be done] on that day unless in a case of necessity, lest something be added or taken away from another; let the question be transmitted for some reasonable cause.

**H**e who wishes to propose any question ought first to well understand the matter—what he wants and what he does not—so that it is not undeliberated, but by the counsel of a discerning free will. He ought to go with good will to the master and devoutly ask counsel from him, telling him the cause of his coming, so that the master himself might be able to understand the clear sign and the matter of the question, the principal figures formed in the inquiry, and how to examine it reasonably and, once examined, to judge it rightly. He should not approach the master with the intent of testing the art, nor should he be someone who tries to tempt [the master], but he should be faithful in all things that ought to be governed. He should [act] so that good counsel can be given to him; for if he is doubtful, it could harm him, especially since God knows the secrets of the heart. It was said to those who sought grace from Him: "Go, your faith has made you whole" <note>original: *fides tua te salvam fecit*; a common Gospel refrain emphasizing that the seeker's spiritual disposition is key to the outcome.</note>. And thus, there can be an error in the judge, but not in the art, because the art is always true in itself and is not falsified by force. The art of the question is sought from the intention; therefore, the seeker ought to speak thus: "Master, I come humbly to you with the faith of love, understanding you to be expert in this art and able to counsel me well. Therefore, I ask you to look well into this matter, so that with your counsel regarding such a thing or such a subject, it may be resolved for me."

**M**aster, wishing to take up the question for judging, should do so benignly...

<meta>This page transitions from the spiritual preparation of the practitioner to the technical rules of geomantic interpretation. It specifically outlines the "Doctrine of the Houses," which assigns different life areas (wealth, family, health, etc.) to specific positions in a geomantic chart. It maintains continuity with the previous page’s discussion on the master's duty to provide counsel.</meta>

[The master] ought to hear the words of the <term>querent</term> <note>the person asking the question</note> and afterward form the question for judgment, and once formed, examine it diligently as the order of the art prescribes and requires. According to how he can best apply the judgment, he ought to calmly judge the question undertaken so that it may benefit him and those who come to his counsel by speaking of both the good and the evil. The question itself should be declared with all hatred and favor set aside, so that for this reason the virtue of his guiding counsel may be recommended.

**I**t must therefore be known that the first <term>figure</term> <note>one of the sixteen symbolic patterns made of dots used in geomancy</note> in every question formed is placed to represent the <term>querent</term> and their fortune as they approach the master concerning the <term>thing sought</term> <note>original: "re quesita"; the specific subject of the divination</note>. The second [figure] in the same chart is placed as the <term>sign of the thing sought</term>, as is done elsewhere; for example:

If the question is concerning the very life of the <term>querent</term>—whether it be good or bad, long or short—then the first <term>figure</term> represents both the <term>querent</term> and the <term>thing sought</term>. | If the question is about profit, the first <term>figure</term> is the <term>querent</term>, but the second is the <term>thing signified</term>. | If it concerns brothers and sisters, or loves and messengers, as is contained in the third <term>house</term> <note>original: "domo"; the positions in a geomantic chart correspond to the twelve houses of astrology</note>, the first <term>figure</term> is for the <term>querent</term> and the third is for the <term>thing sought</term>. | If it concerns fathers and mothers, as is contained in the fourth <term>house</term>, the first <term>figure</term> is for the <term>querent</term> and the fourth is for the <term>thing sought</term>. | If the question is about a son or daughter, or about clothing, or a promised gift, as is contained in the fifth <term>house</term>, the first <term>figure</term> is for the <term>querent</term> and the fifth is for the <term>thing sought</term>. | If the question is about a sick person or a servant, as is contained in the sixth <term>house</term>, the first <term>house</term> is for the <term>querent</term> and the sixth is for the <term>thing sought</term>. | If the question is about a wife, a messenger, an intervention of love, a doctor, a lawsuit, or a <unclear>thief</unclear> <note>original: "latre"; likely "latrone"</note>, as is contained in the seventh <term>house</term>, the first is for the <term>querent</term> and the seventh is for the <term>thing sought</term>. | If the question is about death, fear, the danger of loss, or the guards of <unclear>prisons</unclear>, as is contained in the eighth <term>house</term>, the first is for the <term>querent</term> and the eighth is for the <term>thing sought</term>. | If the question is about a journey, a messenger, letters, or priests, as is contained in the ninth <term>house</term>, the first is for the <term>querent</term> and the ninth is for the <term>thing sought</term>. | If the question is about a lord, the gaining of honor, or medicine, as is contained in the tenth <term>house</term>, the first is for the <term>querent</term> and the tenth is for the <term>thing sought</term>. | If the question is about a friend, profit, a hoped-for and beloved thing, or fortune, as is contained in the eleventh <term>house</term>, the first <term>house</term> is for the <term>querent</term> and the eleventh is for the <term>thing sought</term>. | If, however, it is about someone placed in prison, those bound in <unclear>chains</unclear> <note>original: "vinctis"</note>, or someone placed in exile, as is contained in the twelfth <term>house</term>, the first <term>house</term> is for the <term>querent</term> and the twelfth is for the <term>thing sought</term>.

3 **G**eomancy tells what is to be overcome, and by its tenor, it says the same.

<meta>This page transitions from the specific rules of the "Houses" to a foundational definition of the science of geomancy itself. It explains the etymology of the term, categorizes the sixteen figures based on their astrological and elemental properties, and begins a section on the professional conduct and physical environment required for a practitioner to perform a reading.</meta>

Geomancy <note>original: "geomancia"</note> [comes] from *ge* in Greek, as *ageos* which is interpreted in Latin as "earth," and from *magos* which is "divination." Thus, geomancy is "earthly divination." It is a science that deals with the natural elements in four <term>figures</term> <note>the basic patterns of dots used in this system</note>—namely air, earth, water, and fire—whose virtues provide a clear doctrine for many sciences concerning the dispositions of the past and the future. For this reason, it is one of [four] equal branches: namely <term>pyromancy</term> <note>divination by fire</note> from fire, <term>aeromancy</term> <note>divination by air</note> from air, <term>hydromancy</term> <note>divination by water</note> from water, and <term>geomancy</term> from earth.

**C**oncerning the figures mentioned before, what they are and of what kind they are, it will suffice to run through them all in the table placed above. Their names are found there, along with other qualities: such as some being good, some bad, and some middling; those that are <term>mobile</term> <note>changeable</note> and <term>fixed</term>; those that are "joined" and those that are "light"; those that are fast and those that are slow; <term>entering</term> and <term>exiting</term>; strong and weak; eastern, southern, and northern; as well as those that act as signs of the ecliptic <note>the Zodiac</note> and those that act as planets. These things are named so that the differences between them may be thoroughly known, for reasons found within the figures. Some figures represent only an element, some represent goodness or malice, some lightness, speed or slowness throughout the world. Some represent signs [of the zodiac] and others represent planets.

<margin>the figure</margin>
And the reason why some of the figures are "strong," such as the twelve, and some are "weak," such as the four, is said to be because the twelve figures represent the twelve signs of the heavens <note>the twelve signs of the Zodiac</note>, which do not move from their position for any reason of increase or decrease, like the earth depicted upon the circle of the sphere. The other four, however, are called "weak" because they change themselves and are mixed in a twofold manner of increase and decrease, just as the elements do when they are mixed with one another. These follow a middle path so that this knowledge may be useful for the <term>judgment of questions</term> <note>the final interpretation of the divination</note> which are figured and judged as declared above.

<margin>the figure</margin>
**A**nyone wishing to inquire in this art with honor and utility ought to observe this method which I set down here: he ought to live honestly and cleanly in his house and entryways, which should be places well-disposed to receive the people who come to him. He should have at hand whatever is necessary for his work. He ought to hear the questions kindly [and for a fair] price. Having heard the question—which is the matter at hand—he ought to "raise" the figure in an orderly way, first upon paper with ink, or upon a plaster board, or even in clean sand in a well-polished place. And in raising it, he ought to "sow" lines of points by chance, following the method of geomancy according to a certain quantity of their number, which he must arrange into four lines.

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for geomancy, moving from the definitions of the science to the specific mechanics of generating a geomantic chart (the "formation of the question") and the mathematical rules for verifying its accuracy.</meta>

There are sixteen [points]. Thus, in whatever companion and whatever neighboring [line] they have, the lines of points must be linked two by two, until the last two; those that remain must be reduced to one if only one remains. One must fix the final point until the entire figure is formed. Once formed, it is placed first. And let the <term>querent</term> <note>the person asking the question</note> accept it as the thing properly sought, just as the question brings knowledge and mention of the matter. And as in the judgments of the <unclear>pope</unclear> <note>original: "papi"; possibly a reference to an authority or a scribal error for "mappae" (the map/chart)</note> it is to be judged, so it should be known that the eight figures on the right side represent the querent and those assisting them; the remaining eight represent the thing sought. The <term>Judge</term> <note>the 15th figure in a geomantic chart, which provides the final answer</note> is what is called the fifteenth figure.

# If one asks about the sign that was through all things and why, I say that:
This is the key through which the four points are known, which signify the four elements: namely fire <image-desc>Geomantic figure with red dots: two dots, one dot, one dot, two dots (Fortuna Major)</image-desc>, air <image-desc>Geomantic figure with red dots: two dots, one dot, two dots, one dot (Albus)</image-desc>, water <image-desc>Geomantic figure with red dots: one dot, two dots, two dots, one dot (Conjunctio)</image-desc>, and earth <image-desc>Geomantic figure with red dots: one dot, two dots, one dot, two dots (Fortuna Minor)</image-desc>. It must be said that the first figure represents the East, the second the West, the third the South, and the fourth the North.

->On the method of knowing whether we have formed the question well or not, and by what way it is proven if there is an error there or not<-

Once the question is formed through fifteen figures, before you judge anything by it, look at the Judge, that is, the fifteenth figure. If it was a <unclear>diverse</unclear> figure, it means that it is erroneous in some part. First, in the <unclear>middle</unclear>, all those judging are wise; they are generated first, and then the error and the location of the error [are found]... This is a way of knowing if the processes [are correct]; if the <term>Witnesses</term> <note>the 13th and 14th figures that precede the Judge</note> were even and otherwise were odd, then it is a sign that you have erred. Because of this, it proceeds through the same [steps]: first preparing the points of the "generation of budding" <note>likely referring to the creation of the 'Daughter' figures from the 'Mothers'</note>. The figures [numbered] four, six, seven, eleven, and twelve are on the right. And naturally, there are born from the first six figures those called <term>Daughters</term> <note>figures 5 through 8 in a chart, derived from the first four 'Mothers'</note>. That is, from the fourth, sixth, seventh, eighth, eleventh, and twelfth... they are produced from the four <term>Mothers</term> <note>the first four figures of the chart</note>, as is clear in this example. The first [line] of the points of the fourteenth figure takes its action from the... the second order from the sixth, the third from the seventh. Wherefore the order from the eighth... in this way, if the tenth figure was first of the points, the first order of points of the eighth figure has two points. If it is the fifth figure, they bring forth a diversity of points; the first order on the right witness has only one point. And this method preserves the time... publicly found in the <unclear>proposal</unclear>. The method of the right witness: they have from the four Daughters the first witness; they have from the four figures called Mothers [the second witness], and thus the proposed method is proven. I have proven it: if both witnesses [agree], then it is well done; if not, there is an error.

# Concerning the fifteenth figure, which is called the Judge

Note: if it is asked why the fifteenth figure in [this] part must be even:
We say that since it is born from two witnesses, it has this virtue in whatever way [it is formed].

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for geomancy, specifically addressing the mathematical verification of the 15th figure (the Judge) and the classification of the sixteen figures according to the elements and their qualities of movement.</meta>

Both are naturally even in points in the part of <term>the Judge</term> <note>original: "Di."; likely an abbreviation for "Iudex," the 15th figure</note>; they cannot produce an unequal Judge. If they are equal, they produce an even sum; if they are unequal, they produce one point <note>this refers to the geomantic rule where two even lines or two odd lines result in an even line, while one of each results in an odd line</note>. This is why the 15th figure cannot be odd, but must altogether be even. Therefore, if it is odd, it is false in some part of the preceding figures. If one <term>Witness</term> <note>the 13th and 14th figures used to create the Judge</note> is odd and the other was even, then it is said that there is an error above in the figures. Wherefore, if the Witnesses are discordant in parity or in disparity, it is a sign that an error was made in some figure above, following the natural course. If this occurs, it must be resolved by the fault of the master, who erred in that single figure alone, and thus it will be a fault deserving of penalty.

**I**t should be known that these geomantic figures are only sixteen and no more nor fewer, because of the two possibilities for each of the four elements. Each element has its own figure: namely **Fire** <image-desc>cluster of four red dots in a 2x2 square</image-desc>, **Air** <image-desc>cluster of four red dots in a vertical column</image-desc>, **Water** <image-desc>cluster of four red dots in a diamond shape</image-desc>, and **Earth** <image-desc>cluster of four red dots in a 2x2 square</image-desc>. For this reason, these four primary figures are accepted and called "simple" because they only have four points <note>referring to the four lines that make up a standard geomantic figure</note>. The remaining twelve naturally represent the twelve signs of the heavens <note>the Zodiac</note>. Because twelve figures are halfway above the earth and twelve are halfway in the <unclear>firmament</unclear>, I speak in God's name concerning the figures: six of them are direct and <unclear>fixed</unclear>, where one is the contradictory of the other, as they are called appropriately. Likewise, we say of the figures that six are **Entering** and **Fixed**, and six are **Exiting** and **Mobile**. Which ones these are is clear in the table above. And I say by grace why some are Entering and Fixed and why some are Exiting and Mobile: we say this is because of the motion of the heavens. Those figures that are above the earth representing entering are direct and fixed, and those that are exiting are <unclear>highest</unclear> and mobile because they do not preserve their state. For those that are below the earth are mobile and exiting, but are guided above the earth by another similarity of their kind; and thus above the earth they are fixed and direct, of which this is the example:

Wherefore we say that the sixteen figures <note>In geomancy, there are 16 possible arrangements of single and double dots</note> are sixteen naturally; these signify the beginning and the end of things from which, being joined together, they signify the whole body and soul. Therefore, since each figure signifies its own member <note>original: "mbrū"; referring to a body part</note>, take the strength of the name from the exercise: the first [figure corresponds to] the head, the second the throat, and so on down to the feet. Therefore, if you wish to foreknow the condition of the head, look to the first figure; for the throat, the second, and so on.

## How a figure should be examined, and so for the rest

Note that in every question formed, the four angles <note>The "Angles" are the four most powerful houses in a chart: the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th</note> must always be examined, as must all the remaining parts, and how the figures in those places are friendly to one another by reason of the elements, or by reason of the signs and planets. One must see where one figure is better or worse than the others, whether in goodness or malice, strength or weakness. There is a greater number in the sixteen figures that form the circle of the heavens, and through them, for the witnesses and the judge. It is true that the witnesses and the judge must be well examined with full intention, for the timing depends upon it. It is established that the **Right Witness** <note>original: "testz dextr̄"; the figure representing the person asking the question</note> signifies the petitioner, while the **Left Witness** <note>original: "testz sinister"; the figure representing the matter or person asked about</note> signifies the power of the matter sought. The **Judge** indicates the essence of the matter—namely, whether the thing sought will come to pass, and whether it will happen quickly or slowly. Judgment must be given according to the form and the better or worse state of the question formed.

### If it is asked why four angles are required in every question

We say because they are like the four columns in the four natural structures upon which everything stands; in them resides the greatest power, strength, and stability of every single thing. If it is asked why two witnesses are required in every question, we say that since each part <unclear>testifies</unclear> through its own witness, it shows by its own power what its nature is regarding that about which the question is made. If it is asked why the Judge is so strongly required in every question, they say it is because there is no difference between the petitioner and the thing requested, and since one part is generated from the other part, the Judge holds the place that terminates and defines all that is, and all that arises from the conflict between both parts—namely, the petitioner and the matter of the question.

## Which figures are called angles, succedents, and cadents

Note that the location of the houses of the figures signifies the same thing; whence there is a difference. Certain figures are stronger because they are naturally in the four "exits" <note>likely referring to the four cardinal directions or 'angles'</note>: four are **Angles**, four are **Succedents** <note>houses that "follow" the angles: 2, 5, 8, 11</note>, and four are **Cadents** <note>houses that "fall away" from the angles: 3, 6, 9, 12</note>. If it is asked which places are the Angles, we say the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th; in these places, the figures are said to be stronger than all others. But if a strong figure is required in those places, it is said to be...

Accidental strengthening <note>original: "fortificatio ex accidenti"; a technical term for when a figure gains power due to its position rather than its inherent nature</note>, and therefore it is stronger, just as with horses through [this] strengthening.
According to the diagram <note>original: "grāmā", likely for diagramma</note>, it appears that on the right there are two ill-willed places, namely the Succedents and the Cadents. It should be known that the Angle <note>The "Angles" (1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses) are the most powerful positions in a geomantic chart</note> signifies all things that are always in action and presenting themselves. The Succedents <note>Houses 2, 5, 8, and 11, which "follow" the Angles</note> signify things that do not yet exist but ought to happen and can come to pass. The Cadents <note>Houses 3, 6, 9, and 12, which "fall away" from the Angles</note> signify things that have passed and gone or are coming to an end. As for the four figures which are called Angles, Succedents, and Cadents: the first group of figures—that is, the 1st, 4th, 7th, and 10th houses—are the Angles. The second group—the 5th, 8th, and 11th—are the Succedents. The 3rd, 6th, 9th, and 12th are the Cadent figures. Likewise, the Angles signify public matters or those that can easily become public; the Succedents signify private matters. The Cadents signify the past through [already] publicized points. Whence, just as there are three types [of time]—namely present, past, and future—so is the sign of time prefigured in the form of a man. Therefore, every figure in the order of the twelve <note>The twelve "houses" of the geomantic chart, modeled on the zodiac</note> signifies time, but the figures of the Witnesses and the Judge <note>The Witnesses and Judge are the final figures in a geomantic chart, derived from the others to provide the final answer</note> do not pertain to the signification of time because they are outside the celestial circle.

**F**igures are of certain types: some are entering <note>original: "intrantes"</note> and some are "great" <note>likely meaning significant or stable</note> according to each thing about which a question is formed; a brief and clear example of all these is given here.

**N**ote that of the figures, some are good, some are bad, and some are of middling quality. In their goodness and malice, some are entering, some are exiting <note>original: "exeuntes"</note>, some are benevolent, and some are malevolent; some are fortunate and some are unfortunate; some are strong and some are weak. All of this is shown above in the table of figures.

<margin>Note</margin> It should be known that every entering figure is good and signifies an abundance of things, namely of wheat, barley, possessions, and various goods. Every exiting figure is bad, except for **Joy** <note>original: "leticia", the geomantic figure Laetitia</note>, which is a good figure. It is the figure of **Jupiter** <note>original: "iouis"</note> and it is said that by the grace of God, it is an exception among the class of exiting figures, which are generally [bad] compared to all entering figures. 

Whence, entering figures signify the arrival of things and increases in good, bringing good from the outside into the house, and the petitioner will obtain what they lack. But exiting figures diminish the good coming to the house; they carry it outside and bear away the good that was coming.

Therefore, it must be said that every figure has a nature according to the elements <note>original: "genij elementorum"</note>, and there is no root [of agreement] between enemies, such as a figure of **Water** versus a figure of **Fire**, or a figure of **Earth** versus a figure of **Air**, as there is an open incompatibility of nature. And for a similar reason, this must be said regarding all figures held in relation to the matter being asked.

<margin>Note</margin> And we say that an entering figure is one that has more points at the top or in its middle than it has at its ends <note>Geomantic figures are made of four lines of one or two dots; "entering" figures typically have more dots in the top two lines</note>, as for example here: :. :: :. <note>The scribe uses dot patterns to illustrate the visual "weight" of the figures</note>. For if it is divided through the middle, it has more points above than at the ends, signifying a return. The opposite is true of an exiting figure; a figure is called "exiting" when it has more points at the ends of the figure, namely in its [bottom] half, such as **Lesser Fortune** <note>original: "fortuna minor"</note>: :. :. ::

<margin>General Rule</margin> Every entering figure is a good sign because it signifies entry, and every exiting figure is a bad sign because it signifies exit. However, there are neutral figures which are neither [inherently] entering nor exiting. In a judgment, there are three [such figures] which sometimes signify entry and sometimes exit, according to their "society" <note>The "Company" (societas) refers to how a figure relates to the one next to it in the geomantic chart</note> and where they are located. For a cause may happen to two figures—whether fortunate or unfortunate, good or bad—based on the place, the society, and the aspect <note>A term borrowed from astrology referring to the geometric relationship between positions</note> of all the figures. Therefore, one must look at

<margin>Regarding the affinity of the houses</margin> the hour, the goodness, and the malice of both the places <note>the "houses" or positions in the chart</note> and the figures, just as one must judge whether it is good or bad. For if a good figure is found in a good place, then the sign is perfect and honorable. But if a good figure is in a bad place, then the figure loses some of its goodness because of the accidental malice of the place; thus the place overcomes the good figure because it is [unsuitable]. We say the same regarding a bad figure in a good place. But if the place is good and the figure is good, then that good is perfect in every way. Likewise, regarding those that are...

**Despair** <note>original: "Desperacio". Note that the scribe uses the name "Despair" for the figure traditionally called "Puer" (The Boy). For this reason, figures are mobile because of their mobility, fixed because of their stability, and **common** <note>original: "zmūis" for "communis"</note> because of their shared nature or the middle ground of their shape. Whether figures are fixed or mobile is clear from above. ¶ Concerning the question of which are the common figures, we say there are four:

All **mobile** figures signify a mobile thing; **fixed** figures signify a stable thing with slowness; **common** figures signify a middle ground between speed and slowness. Note then that which is more accelerated or slowed down is according to its own weakness; for it is true that a weak man cannot sustain himself for long under labor. And so these are the causes of the figures, according to the doctrine and better instruction for the memory of those things which are necessary for a man in the judgment of figures. In the judgment of the aforesaid figures, he may be able to recognize the art of the figures in every quality. Let this suffice for the description of the causes; now follows the description of the figures.

Note that the first authors who discovered this art, with a certain facility and out of a great natural genius, took the unformed figures of the stars of the heaven. They did not take all of them—especially those in the higher circles—because of the extreme confusion of their signs. Instead, they took only some of those found within the zodiacal circle, which is the path of the sun. Therefore, the figures of this art are not simple points made at the whim of the practitioners; rather, they arise from the voice of nature and from the forms of the stars in the higher heavens to this state of figuring. Just as the stars of heaven, the signs of the zodiac, and the four elements are all arranged in the hour of birth, these figures are made in the likeness and form of the celestial bodies. Thus, although they may often appear to be points, they are not simple points but ought to be regarded as stars. They exist in the likeness of the stars of heaven, which are like fixed points in the sky itself, unlike our points marked on paper or parchment by an abacus <note>a tool for calculation or drawing</note>; yet they possess the power of signifying that which governs the entire day based on the question that is formed.

# Knowledge of the Twelve Houses in All Their Variations

<margin>This figure is bad; what follows is the table <note>original: "mare," literally 'sea,' likely referring to a large chart or 'map'</note> to read the rulers of the houses.</margin> The heavens naturally possess twelve equal parts, which are said to contain the locations of the planets. The measure of these <term>planetary houses</term> <note>These are the twelve divisions of the sky used in astrology and geomancy to represent different areas of life, such as wealth, health, or travel</note> is determined by the twelve signs of the zodiac through their centers. In these twelve parts, each one is called a "sign," and thus every location in the heavens—and every moment in time—has its own house. Just as a sign holds a place as a dwelling or house, the planets are like the lords and rulers of these houses. Regarding the houses themselves, they are of equal size, each consisting of thirty degrees <note>original: "xxx [gradus]"</note> and no more. However, they are distinguished by the different qualities of the <term>elements</term> <note>Earth, Air, Fire, and Water</note>, which define each sign in a special way. Therefore, just as there is a great difference between the elements—where one is better or worse than another—so it is with the houses of heaven.

¶ For this reason, it should be known that some houses of heaven are good, some are just beginning <note>original: "inchoatis," meaning preparatory or mediocre</note>, and some are excellent. Conversely, among them, some are bad, others worse, and others the worst of all. In every house, there are certain stars noted by the wise from which <term>geomantic figures</term> <note>The 16 patterns of dots used in this divination system</note> are formed. The better houses are the 3rd and the 5th; the best are the 10th and the 11th. The bad houses are namely the 2nd, 6th, 8th, and 12th. It should be noted that the 1st, 11th, 10th, 9th, and 8th belong to the <term>Midheaven</term> <note>original: "medium celi," the highest point of the sky</note> and the left part of the chart. The first house is the ruler and is called the <term>Ascendant</term> <note>The house rising on the eastern horizon at the time of the reading</note>. The other figures follow the right side of the heavens, and the 7th house is called the opposite of the Ascendant. Among those above, the 6th is bad, the 8th is worse, and the 12th is the worst. This must be understood as the quality of the place itself, which is declared through the figure placed within it. Whether the figure is praised or blamed depends entirely on the divine nature of the house, according to whether it is good or bad.

This is the opinion of many, and it is also mine: ¶ The **Houses** that are good are the 1st, 5th, 10th, and 11th. The bad houses are the 6th, 12th, 8th, and 2nd. The mediocre ones are the 3rd, 4th, 7th, and 9th. Regarding the primary houses: the 1st is <term>Eastern</term> <note>orientalis</note>, the 7th is <term>Western</term> <note>occidentalis</note>, the 10th is <term>Southern</term> <note>meridionalis</note>, and the 4th is <term>Northern</term> <note>septentrionalis</note>. Thus, just as the 7th is the degree of the 1st, so the 3rd is the degree of the 10th and 9th in combination. **And** the usefulness of these things for the body is great for judging well. Since in geomancy there are good, bad, and mediocre houses, if a good figure is found in a good house, then it signifies something good and gives a good testimony for whatever matter is signified in that place. Conversely, if a bad figure is in a bad place, it indicates a poor outcome. The truth is known by contrast: when a good figure is in a bad place (like a bad house) or when a bad figure is found in a good house. Therefore, a good figure found in a good house doubles the positive meaning.

For perhaps when all things are considered, they tend toward the first position by way of good affection or harmony, or conversely, through discord. But those figures that are in aspect are not the primary actors; rather, they are helpers and strengtheners of their own side.

¶ You must know that if a figure, through its aspect, strongly supports its side, one may contradict the other. For this reason, it should be well noted which figures—whether good or bad—are located in a particular place. For good figures are always good, and bad ones bad. If any figure is found to be repeated twice or more, it is a sign that it does not change its basic judgment or the meaning of the matter from what it signified in its first location. <margin>S</margin> However, it does change the **outcome** <note>original: "effectus"</note>; therefore, by the difference of the places into which they move, one must deduce whether the result will be good or evil. The same must be noted regarding the "master of the gathering" in your interpretation, because one figure strengthens another; if it is a good figure, it strengthens well, but if it is bad, it will strengthen poorly.

¶ It should also be known that all figures are "social" <note>original: "sociales"; referring to the pairing of houses in geomantic reading</note> in this manner: the figure placed in the first house creates a partnership with the second. One is called the companion of the other because they form this society together. Thus, the same figure is a companion to the second, the third to the fourth, and so on for the others. ¶ However, the partnership of figures is determined by following this order of pairings: the **second** with the **first**; the **fourth** with the **third**; the **sixth** with the **fifth**; the **eighth** with the **seventh**; the **twelfth** with the **eleventh**; the **tenth** with the **ninth**; and the **thirteenth** with the **fourteenth**. ...with speed. ¶ The **seventh figure** <note>original: "vijª fig̃a"; referring to the Seventh House</note> signifies the autumn season; regarding the age of man, it signifies youth, from the twenty-fifth year up to the fiftieth; regarding the effect of a work, it signifies slowness and laziness. ¶ The **fourth figure** <note>the Fourth House</note> signifies the winter season; regarding the age of man, it signifies old age; regarding the effect of deeds, it signifies slowness, unless harmony or discord among the figures completes it. The second, fifth, eighth, and eleventh figures are **succedent** <term>succedent</term> <note>original: "succedẽtes"; houses that "follow" the angles; they represent resources and stability</note>, and these places are less strong; they signify public things and secret matters. The sixth, third, ninth, and twelfth figures are **cadent** <term>cadent</term> <note>original: "cadent̃"; houses that "fall away" from the angles; usually considered the weakest or most problematic positions</note> and are weak places for good, but very strong for evil; they signify all hidden matters <note>original: "secta"</note>.

I say that every first figure, in its nature, is like a man newly born into the world who is young and wishes to act as much as he can; he is like a man fighting from the start, who thinks of fighting with every man who wishes to contradict him, and wants to see if he finds anyone resisting him or wanting to prove whether he is good and powerful. Therefore, this is the **first cause**, and for that reason it is called the **Ascendant** <note>original: "ascēdēs"; the starting point of the chart representing the person asking the question</note>, corresponding to the natural figure of the world, for all that is like a man who is ready for battle with another and can exert all his strength against him; hence the stronger is seen over the weak.

Note that every figure is, by its element, a natural friend to its own kind, like a brother or sister of the same blood. Therefore, where there is similarity in the figures, there is friendship and harmony, but where there is dissimilarity, there is enmity. A sufficient example of this is seen in the harmony of figures: those that follow one another are like two brothers in blood in their love for each other. <image-desc>Two identical geomantic figures side-by-side in red ink. Each consists of four rows of dots: 2 dots, 2 dots, 1 dot, 1 dot (Fortuna Major, "Greater Fortune").</image-desc> These figures that follow one another are as two primary enemies hating each other in all things: <image-desc>Two identical geomantic figures side-by-side in black ink. Each consists of four rows of dots: 2 dots, 1 dot, 1 dot, 2 dots (Albus, "White").</image-desc> **Albus** <image-desc>Repeat of the two previous black geomantic figures (Albus).</image-desc> These that follow are as two men who love each other from the start, such as: <image-desc>Two identical geomantic figures side-by-side in red ink. Each consists of four rows of dots: 1 dot, 2 dots, 2 dots, 1 dot (Puella, "The Girl").</image-desc> Thus is the friendship of the aspects: the first figure sees and loves that which is before it, up to the fourth and fifth; it also loves and delights in seeing the seventh, tenth, eleventh, and twelfth. For the first figure is like a sister to the eleventh, not merely as a friend but as a sister. The other figures, however, the first neither sees nor loves, namely the sixth, seventh, eighth, and twelfth <note>The text repeats some numbers; this refers to "blind" houses that do not form a traditional geometric "aspect" to the first house</note>. The reason is that they all hold each other in hatred and harm and contradict one another... the fifth and eighth are the seekers; the sixth and seventh are the matters.

<meta>This page continues the technical breakdown of the twelve houses in astrology and geomancy, moving from the general classification of the houses to their specific significations in the life and body of the "querent" (the person asking the question). In the **first natural house** <note>original: "prima domo naturali"</note>, every person may inquire about their entire body or seek after health; it concerns the beginning and the head for all first mortal members of things, with the whole heart which one desires. It speaks of the natural face and the state of the body of those being born and already born. It also concerns the **imagination, intelligence, and memory**; it is the **Ascendant** <term>Ascendant</term> <note>the sign or point rising on the eastern horizon at the moment of birth or the asking of a question</note>, the person of the seeker, the rising of the east, properly the first of each thing, or the first person in all things, which is treated in the first way by the actors and passions. And it is the **Joy of the Moon** <note>original: "gaudium lune"; in traditional astrology, each planet "rejoices" in a specific house where its influence is most comfortable</note>. Here, regarding what one seeks in the first house from the aforesaid matters—for example—whether they seek anything regarding their life, what kind it might be and what it will be; whether through some fate they may have a better or worse mind; and whether the beginning of such a matter will be good or bad for them.

In the **second house**, these things are considered: everything that ought to happen in the coming week; whether there will be some profit or not; whether from such a business deal that one wishes to make, they ought to gain profit or not; whether they ought to receive money for the year from such a source; whether a thing that was lost is in the house or not; whether such a household servant is faithful to the master or not; whether money which one wishes to deposit with another will be well-secured or not; or concerning the type of household goods in movable merchandise which are present. One seeks the cause in riches or all things which are under their dominion, and the expense for weapons, etc.

In the **third house**, these things are considered: whether a sister or a brother, a companion or a neighbor, is good for them; secrets in a physical act, or likewise the **throat** <note>original: "gulam"; the third house traditionally governs the throat and neck in some systems, or communication</note> of a man; whether his mistress is faithful to him or not, and whether she loves him faithfully or not; concerning rumors, whether they be false; whether it is a disturbance or a falsehood that is new; whether a dream is thus good or bad; which of two brothers might die first; what kind of companion he has, whether to have them with him in all things or outside; what will come of a messenger, a friend, or indeed a brother; a short journey; a sealed letter; the shoulders, arms, and hands.

In the **fourth house**, these things are considered: whether a person is loved by others or by friends or not; whether good **ancestral estates** <note>original: "patrimonia"</note> ought to be increased or not; whether a lost or hidden thing ought to ever be recovered; whether treasure is in such a place or not; whether it is good to found a house or not, or a **palace** <note>original: "pallaxium," a variant of "palatium"</note> in such a place; whether that which they begin ought to be happily completed or not; in what part of such a place such a thing or treasure might be; which person is a fugitive, or something else lost; or the time for any matter; for all women, their life and stability; to hold a true matter at night; the chest and the stomach.

The **Right Witness** <note>original: "Ostis" is a scribal error for "Testis," meaning witness</note> is not called a "master," but here it represents the parents from whom it originates; it signifies the effect they have on all the superior figures from which they are generated in the lineage. The **Left Witness** <note>original: "Testis sinister"</note> is also not called a "master," but is placed here for grace and essence; it signifies the effect they have on all the superior figures from which they are generated in the lineage.

---

Every right-hand figure signifies an ill omen through the four figures separated at the sides; therefore it is not called the master, but the **Judge** <note>The "Iudex" is the final figure produced by combining the two Witnesses</note> from the left-hand types and all those things that were in the lineage; thus it looks back and pertains to them expressly.

---

The **sixteenth figure** is the "judicial" figure, which is called **artificial** <note>meaning derived through method rather than appearing naturally in the first twelve houses</note> because it comes from the two natural figures among the twelve; and this naturally represents what must fully be resolved by its own nature at the end, according to the matter of their parents or that which is being asked; this happens naturally in the time of the parents.

**Jupiter** is a planet, not a [fixed] star, which is signified by these two figures:

# **The Sun**
The **Sun** is a planet and not a [fixed] star, and it is signified by these two figures: **Greater Fortune** <image-desc>geomantic figure: Fortuna Major (:: . .)</image-desc> and **Lesser Fortune** <image-desc>geomantic figure: Fortuna Minor (. . ::)</image-desc>. This [the Sun] is always good in every place through **Greater Fortune**, and evil through **Lesser Fortune**. Therefore, it ought to be called good through **Greater Fortune** and to signify well, representing a great good and success <note>original: "egerano," likely a corruption of a term for profit or gain</note> through **Greater Fortune**.

Through **Lesser Fortune**, it signifies the earth and every lazy, slow, stable, and firm thing through **Greater Fortune**. But in a birth chart <note>original: "geniu[m] natalu[m]"</note>, it signifies a noble and powerful man, such as a counselor to kings <note>original: "tossiru regu[m]," likely a corruption of "consiliarium"</note> and of men, and so forth. It signifies a good man, but through **Lesser Fortune** it is altogether evil, and likewise for health and for masters.

⸬ <note>The symbol of four dots represents the geomantic figure Populus (The People), which is associated here with the Moon.</note> If at birth it signifies a good cleric, a wise and literate man, a man of knowledge and subtlety; a writer, a painter, a poor cleric, and a priest of the church; perceived according to much and good sagacity, and one who delights in beautiful and clean things, and is pleasing to others. <margin>P</margin> <note>Likely 'P' for Populus</note>
The **Moon** is pleasing, not a [fixed] star, and is much inclined toward being pleasing and [adjusting] to the nature of the places where it is present. Where it is in [good] houses, the man is good; in [bad] houses, he is evil. And a man is spoken of according to its disposition in his age and in the location of the houses. <meta>This page transitions from the general astrological properties of planets and signs discussed on the previous page to the specific rules of geomancy. <margin>Aspects</margin>
The **aspect** <note>In both astrology and geomancy, an "aspect" is the angle or distance between two points, which determines how they influence each other.</note> is said to be triple. There are [various] degrees: the **sextile**, the **square** <note>original: "iiij[or]," referring to the 90-degree angle of the fourth house</note>, and the **opposition**, which consists of one hundred and eighty degrees. The sextile, however, is sixty degrees before and sixty degrees after [the primary position]. The square is the fourth degree <note>meaning the fourth house or 90 degrees</note>, and after that the opposition holds the 180th degree. <insert>This</insert> should be known: that every figure nevertheless accidentally preserves a "friendship" <note>An affinity or positive relationship between two positions.</note> through its power, and such a square indicates a character of habit; for it is not permitted to pass over this, but to fix one's place, as there is friendship from one place to another. 

A **conjunction** occurs when the first figure is in the second place, just as the first and second houses are neighbors or next to each other; any of these is said to be in the first and same degree with its figure through a joining; then it is strong and powerful because it occupies so many places in the heavens. But if another figure is joined through faith below, as in a joining, then the second place belongs to many persons; if it is the fifth, it is not said to be of the same degree. Therefore, they ought to work together. 

The **sextile** [aspect] is said to occur when the same [influence] is in the third [place], through which the first is related; the sextile is the 3rd figure, as well as the 13th <note>Geomantic charts usually involve 12 houses plus extra "witness" and "judge" figures; the 13th is the First Witness.</note>, and this aspect is often good, yet pertains to affection. 

The **square** aspect <note>original: "Quadrans"</note> occurs when a figure is in the 4th [house], as well as the 11th; this aspect is moderately good or bad, according to whether evil or good is being done, toward the 7th and the 1st houses. 

The **trine** aspect occurs when a figure is in the 5th and 8th houses; this aspect is perfectly good toward the first, since there is joy in the first and the same [place] when the first figure is seen at the 5th; it changes things not a little and is said to be well-disposed because it is in your joy, especially if the figure itself is good. 

The **opposition** aspect occurs when a figure is in the 7th house, because every figure in the 7th is the generic [opposite] of the first figure; this applies to the whole second place of the figure, not the degree of the figure, unless by chance there is a "birth" <note>original: "genitura," likely referring to the way a figure is generated or duplicated in the chart.</note> of the first figure for the whole time. Hence, there is a perfect aspect everywhere when the same figure is there, or a "birth" through its own generation, even if through another, such as dissimilar forms or elements. For example, if the boundary is <image-desc>Geomantic figure Carcer: two dots, one dot, one dot, two dots.</image-desc> and the boundary is <image-desc>Geomantic figure Conjunctio: one dot, two dots, two dots, one dot.</image-desc> or if the boundary is <image-desc>Geomantic figure Via: one dot, one dot, one dot, one dot.</image-desc> and in the 4th house is the same figure <image-desc>Geomantic figure Populus: two dots, two dots, two dots, two dots.</image-desc> and it does not cease after other places in the boundaries <image-desc>Geomantic figure Acquisitio: one dot, one dot, two dots, two dots.</image-desc> this is one aspect.

### On the Five Varieties of Geomancy in Any Question

<margin>9</margin>
There are indeed five ways by which the nature of any figure is varied in any question of fortune. First, by knowing the "darkness" <note>original: "tenebre," likely referring to the hidden or "shadow" influences remaining in a chart calculation.</note> that remains. Second, by knowing the nature of its **generation** <note>How the figure was created through the process of marking dots.</note>. Third, by knowing the properties of the figure, as in their nature... how they are produced. Fourth, according to the **movement** which the figures make through the houses: whether they leave behind good things and change into bad ones, or the reverse; or if they leave behind a malevolent influence and join with a benevolent one. Fifth, according to the figures appearing through the places before and after them. For these ought to be likened to tones... so that one may better judge the matter which is sought...

<margin>p</margin>

### On Considering the Goodness and Badness of Figures in Any Question

The **goodness** and **badness** of figures can be according to the nature of the figure itself and according to the place <note>The "house" or position in the chart.</note> where it is found. For of the figures, some are **good**, some are **best**; others indeed are **bad**, and some are **worst**, both by their nature and by accident <note>A figure might be "naturally" good but "accidentally" bad because it is placed in a house of misfortune.</note>. Which figures are good and which are bad, and for what reason, has already been expressed above; and it is expressly determined for what cause [they change] according to their place. A good figure can be placed in a sign that is good or bad; or a good figure located in a good house, such as the 1st or the 10th; a bad one in a bad house, such as the 5th or the 12th <note>While the 5th house is usually positive, the 12th is traditionally the house of hidden enemies and confinement.</note>. Also, in all things, a figure is called by its letter, its **gate** <note>original: "porta," a term for the specific entry point or primary influence a figure exerts.</note>, through which one can easily and clearly recognize its goodness and badness, for the reason stated regarding its own "gate."

## On the "Figure of the Figure" and its Significance

The "Sign of the Figure" is good for those seeking omens because the figure and the place agree. A <term>Figure of the Figure</term> <note>This technical term describes a "domicile" effect: when a figure appears in the house that matches its natural meaning, doubling its strength.</note> is said to occur when a figure is found in the location of its own name; then it is said to **rejoice** and be strong in its own right. Likewise, if a question is asked about **profit** <note>The 2nd House traditionally governs money and moveable goods.</note> and **The Boy** (Puer) <note>geomantic figure of Puer: one dot, two dots, one dot, one dot</note> appears in the second [house], then it is the Figure of the Figure.

If a question is asked about the "sphere of joy" and in the fifth [house]... then there too is the Figure of the Figure. <note>The text here is slightly garbled in the Latin but refers to **Joy** (Laetitia) <note>geomantic figure of Laetitia: one dot, two dots, two dots, two dots</note> appearing in the 5th house of pleasure and children.</note>

<meta>This page continues the technical instructions for evaluating a geomantic chart. The previous page discussed the concept of a figure "rejoicing" when placed in a favorable "angle" or house. This page formalizes how figures are strengthened or weakened based on eight specific conditions and introduces the "motion" of figures—when the same figure appears in multiple houses of a single reading.</meta>

Eight ways there are in which figures are made fortunate and unfortunate: according to their **nature**, **property**, **location**, **aspect**, **association**, **disvariation**, **motion**, and **present unity**. <note>These are the eight criteria a geomancer uses to "weigh" whether a figure gives a positive or negative answer.</note> Regarding **nature**, this is because if there is a concord of elements in their nature—such as when two figures are of the same element—they are strengthened. Regarding **property**, it is when a figure, through its own property, "loves" the place of the matter <note>original: "loco rei"; referring to the specific house that governs the question being asked, such as the House of Wealth for a question about money.</note>. Regarding **location**, it is if a figure agrees with its location and does not cease from seeking out what is required by holding back. Regarding **aspect**, it is when it is compared with the aspect of its own [related figures], namely if the first figure stands in such an aspect to its own through directors or peacemakers <note>In geomancy, "directors" and "peacemakers" are technical terms for figures that help resolve a conflict between two other figures in the chart.</note>. Regarding **association**, it is when the first figure is well or poorly associated in its second location. Regarding **disvariation** <note>original: "disvariacione"; the quality of being different or changing in character.</note>, it is when some figures are diverse and "bound" because they are indirect, and those running through are different in the first place; and by their grace, because the second and third are thus placed in opposition. Regarding **motion**, it is because when the first figure moves itself once or more through the sequence. Regarding **motion of unity**, it is because through the same process, some figures are born from nature—just as from excess—and some from before, because one figure is born and another from an odd point and from a "bad mother" <note>Geomantic figures are generated from four "Mothers." A "bad mother" refers to one of these primary figures that has an inherently negative meaning.</note>. Therefore, it must be examined with a correct judgment.

## On the motion of figures in a formed question

<margin>m</margin>
The rising <note>original: "ortus"; the appearance or generation of the figures in the chart.</note> of the figures allows it to happen by reason of fortune, from which one recognizes that another figure appears more than once. And if this figure is in a "firm hand" <note>original: "manu firma"; a technical term for a figure that is stable or fixed, rather than mobile.</note> in its first location, its nature has placed it there. If, therefore, it is there by its own property, it is the same. But if it has moved itself, the judgment changes as many times as it has moved, because it is more changed, and it is no longer said to be "in its place." Rather, it is in the place where fortune has made its change; and that figure which moves itself is like a stranger who visits many houses, almost with everyone, because they cannot, over time, become friends or parents, since the figure does not remain in one place. And in other places, therefore, if it has changed its place a hundred times, it is in no place at all; and such is the house of a figure that moves itself. The fact that it changes to certain places is so that it may seek counsel or help there, and from such things, they are entirely in that place. And a figure is one with the house when it holds more places; commonly this occurs through strength. Peace is seen in these things, though some things are needed. For when it is in a certain disposition in which it is its own, it is said to be in its element. And therefore it is said that such a figure is strong in its own region, and wherever it is fortunate, it is further said that the figure is more powerful.

<margin>n</margin> **Note** that when unfortunate figures <note>original: "figurae infortunatae"; these are figures like *Amissio* (Loss) or *Carcer* (Prison) that generally carry negative meanings.</note> are found in fortunate houses <note>original: "domibus fortunatis"; the houses in a geomantic chart representing positive areas of life, like the House of Wealth or the House of Success.</note>, they signify the joy of man and the increase of good. If fortunate figures are in unfortunate houses, it is a sign of an imperfect evil, and not entirely so by itself, since some [good] sign is seen to be signified, and therefore there are fears and terrors on account of the appearance; but in these cases the effect is understood because the good cooperates with the good. If, however, it is mitigated by a bad house, the evil is diminished as if restrained; and if the evil is in a good house, then a man has [success], and that [evil] is restrained so that it does not abound as it otherwise would.

### Chapter on the four kinds of powers by which a judgment of good and evil is properly known in general.

<margin>q</margin> **There are four** general types of powers for judging well forever, which are **translation**, **occupation**, **conjunction** <note>original: "iunctio"</note>, and **mutation**. Let us here define each species aptly in order, with its own example. The first is **translation** <term>translation: the "movement" of a figure's influence from one house to another when that same figure is repeated elsewhere in the chart</term>, which is when any second [figure] joins itself, changed into the same figure for the sake of the matter. For example, this is said to happen when the second figure of the matter changes itself into the property of the nearest [figure]; if it was good, it speaks good, and if bad, it speaks evil, as is shown in the example. A certain person asked whether he could contract a marriage with a certain woman, so that he would not lose his previous [status]; such was the result:

### Concerning Knowledge of the Seeker's Part of Fortune and How to Observe It in Every Case

The **Part of Fortune** <term>Pars Fortunae; in geomancy and astrology, this is a calculated point used to determine where the seeker will find luck, prosperity, or the resolution of their problem.</term> is sought on the day of the question and is recognized in many ways, because it is diverse. It has been used in various modes, and the sayings regarding them are some well said, some poorly, and some mediocre. We, however, can better understand this mode that is observed and must be followed.

First, if the questions of fortune are naturally [asked] through the movement of the seeker’s intention, it reveals to him what is possible for him and the times of fortunes which joy indicates. When nothing stands in the way, it should be said that the first [figure] signifies the Part of Fortune entirely in time, if it is in that form there. But if it is changed in the second or the last **houses** <term>domus; the twelve divisions of a geomantic chart, each representing a specific area of life like wealth, family, or health.</term> of the places, it can be shown that the Part of Fortune is already there; and according to the goodness of the place, it should be called good, or bad, or mediocre. For those things which are at rest wander through changing places, and for those who seek fortune, it is said that the question has its place in the proper [houses], and the places are through such properties as the Part itself shall show.

¶ If the first figure stands firm in such a way in its time and place, then the Part of Fortune is for the most part staying both with the seeker himself and nearby. But if it has been changed in the second house, then the Part of Fortune is the response to the seeker regarding what he has and what profit or gain is expected. ¶ But if it enters the third place, then the Part of Fortune is regarding brothers or sisters, or his near relations, or his messengers, or something <margin><image-desc>An ornate calligraphic flourish extends from the text into the left margin.</margin> relating to all the places as the explanation of the houses above signifies.

¶ I say that if the first figure was **mobile** <term>mobilis; a quality of a sign or figure indicating change, speed, or lack of permanence.</term> in this way, the Part of Fortune is to be called mobile according to its sign, just as are the signs of the element and the planet. If, however, it was firm and stable, then it is said to be a stable Part. But if it was **common** <term>communis; also known as "mutable," indicating something that fluctuates or acts as a bridge between states.</term>, then it is often said to wander and will change according to the time and the timing. ¶ If the first figure was mobile, then the seeker's intention is said to be mobile, or it will be perhaps more than what is declared. ¶ But if it was **fixed** <term>fixa; a quality indicating stability, endurance, or a situation that will not change soon.</term>, then it is a Part from which the seeker’s intention does not depart...

# The Figure of the Red One <note>original: "Rubens" or "Rubeus"; this figure is associated with the planet Mars and generally signifies passion, violence, or vice.</note>

**Rubeus** in the first house <note>original: "ī pᵃ do°"; the 1st House represents the person asking the question and their physical body.</note> signifies an evil man, bad intentions, great indignation, fury, the shedding of new blood, audacity, and the permission of a corpse <note>original: "orpete"; likely a corruption of "corpore" or "obreptio" (deception)</note>.
<margin>1.</margin> It leads into disease, quarrels, hatred, envy, the intrusion of force, and the ruin of the body; a crowd of men looking to do harm. Regarding dignities, when it is joined with a horrible [figure], such as <image-desc>Geomantic figure Rubeus: a vertical arrangement of two dots, then one dot, then two dots, then two dots.</image-desc> <note>This figure typically represents "The Red One," though the dots here (2-1-2-2) vary slightly from the standard 1-2-1-1; geomantic manuals often contain regional variations.</note>, it signifies a scourge, killing, and a crowd of painters <note>original: "pictoꝝ"; possibly a scribal error for "peccatorum" (sinners)</note> turned toward evil. But when it is joined with a good [figure], such as <image-desc>Geomantic figure Fortuna Major: a vertical arrangement of two dots, then two dots, then one dot, then one dot.</image-desc> <note>Greater Fortune</note>, it is a sign of all the things predicted above [being mitigated]. ¶ In the second part <note>House 2: Wealth and possessions.</note> of the aforementioned: the gain
