<meta>This page transitions from the general yearly prognostications based on the day of the week to the specific influences of the "planetary hours" (Planetenstunden). While the previous page looked at the year as a whole, this text provides a guide for the "hours" governed by specific celestial bodies, advising the reader on when to begin tasks or expect success.</meta>

The **hour of Venus** <note>original: "Venusz (stund)"</note>; as it is, it is at first strong and hard. If good fortune is to occur, it happens only at the end, particularly in matters involving heirs.

In the **hour of Mars**, there is no good fortune, except perhaps a little at the very end.

The **hour of the Sun** is quite hard and useless, whether one has dealings with a lord or work to perform; whatever one begins at this time will only bring you distress.

The **hour of Venus** is good for all matters and is gracious.

The **hour of Venus**: although it is useful and joyful, it is nevertheless often fickle—like a lady who turns her favor away.

Venus performs the will of Jupiter.

The **hour of Mercury** is good from the beginning until the midpoint, but thereafter it is useless and bad.

The **hour of the Moon** <note>original: "Des monen stund"</note>, from the beginning until the middle, is neither good nor bad. Whatever one begins during this time will not turn out particularly well; after the midpoint, the hour becomes worse, and by the end, it is utterly unfavorable <note>original: "gar ze richt," likely meaning "rightly bad" or "utterly ruinous" in this context</note>.

<meta>This page transitions from the celestial influences of the planetary hours into the practical application of "natural magic" and alchemy. "My God, my God, why hast thou forsaken me?" <note>original Latin/Hebrew: "hely hely lamazabatani"; these are the biblical words of Christ on the cross, here used as a powerful invocation</note> You who sit on high, free me; draw me out from sadness. **Elohim** <note>original: "Eleijm," a Hebrew name for God</note>, Father, [and] Son, may you be blessed. *Soth, He, Vau* <note>Mystical syllables or letters often found in Kabbalistic magic</note>, Eli, Messiah, Savior, Emmanuel, **Sabaoth** <note>Lord of Hosts</note>, **Adonai** <note>Lord</note>, most pious and merciful King, most compassionate pitier and strong one. *Ay, ay, tu norayde* <note>Likely phonetic magical chants or corrupted names</note>, Michael, Gabriel, Raphael, Uriel, Raguel, Seaphiel, Thobiel, Panthaseron, Chel, Phehel, Yait. You, Savior; Mary, mediator, middle, mediatrix... <note>The text appeals to a long list of archangels and the Virgin Mary to assist the practitioner</note>. 

And by the name of God, the **Tetragrammaton** <note>The four-letter Hebrew name of God, YHWH, considered to hold immense power</note>, and by the seventy other names of God, both speakable and unspeakable, in Hebrew, Greek, and Latin, known and unknown to us and others: I adjure you—whatever spirit you are, whether one or many, by whatever name you are called—you who keep the **Martagon herb** <note>Likely the Turk's cap lily (*Lilium martagon*). In alchemical lore, this plant was linked to the planet Mars and believed to facilitate the transmutation of metals</note> hidden from my eyes, that in this instant you trust me and fulfill with help [my request], so that I may see, be able to find, gather, and have the Martagon herb through the omnipotence and virtue of God, to finally carry it away with me and preserve it most securely all the days of my life, through Him who is to come to judge the living and the dead and the world by fire. Amen.

After this, you should sprinkle it with holy water and, having signed it with your right hand, say the same prayer while uprooting it, in the name of the Father, and of the Son, and of the Holy Spirit. Amen.

Take the juice of this herb and make **mercury** <note>quicksilver</note> boil in it, and it will become a **red stone** <note>The "Red Lion" or "Red Stone" is a stage of the Great Work in alchemy, signifying the successful creation of the Philosopher's Stone</note>. Put one part of this stone over a hundred parts of mercury, and it will become **gold** <note>original: "sol" (the Sun), the alchemical symbol for gold</note>. And if you place it over **silver** <note>original: "luna" (the Moon)</note> and molten silver, it converts it into the best gold. From which gold, if one part is placed again over a hundred parts of silver, it becomes gold. And if mercury is boiled in that same water, it is converted into gold, from which gold, if you place it over silver, it will become gold. Likewise, from the root of this herb, congeal <unclear>Mars</unclear> **brass** <note>original: "orichalcum," a legendary golden-colored alloy</note> and it will soften and become good **silver** <note>original: "luna"</note>.

# For the Pestilence

Also<gloss>Item</gloss>, if the pestilence <note>original: "pestilenz"; referring to the bubonic plague.</note> comes upon you, take theriac <note>original: "triax"; a complex medicinal paste used as a universal antidote since antiquity, often containing dozens of ingredients including opium and exotic spices.</note> as large as two beans—it must be of good quality—and sulfur <gloss>schwebel</gloss> as large as one bean. Crush it into a powder and then take your own urine <gloss>harn</gloss>, two or three spoonfuls, and put the theriac and the sulfur into the urine and rub it well together. Drink this up and then lie down warmly in a bed and cover yourself well so that you sweat. And always keep a soaked <note>original: "gebeytz"; likely soaked in vinegar or herbal wine to act as a filter for bad air.</note> slice of bread before your mouth so that the strength <note>original: "matzzij"; likely referring to the vital spirit or the medicinal potency.</note> stays with you; then you will recover without a doubt, provided you do this within the hour that the sickness has struck you.

<margin>For pestilence</margin>
Also<gloss>Item</gloss>, take Armenian bole <note>original: "bolu armenu"; a reddish-brown medicinal clay imported from the East, highly valued as an astringent and antitoxin.</note> as large as a hazelnut and sealed earth <note>original: "terra sigillata"; a specialized medicinal clay pressed into tablets and stamped with an official seal to guarantee its authenticity against poisoning.</note> of the same size. Take good theriac <gloss>triax</gloss> as large as a bean and three tablespoons full of vinegar <gloss>essich</gloss>. Put these pieces into the vinegar and rub them well together, and use this as stated above.

# A whiteness on silver <note>original: "luna"; the alchemical name for silver, associated with the moon.</note> that lasts fifty castings and remains as white as fine silver

<margin>Note.</margin> Take vitriol <note>A sulfate mineral, likely iron or copper sulfate, used for its acidic properties.</note> and alum, one lot <note>A historical unit of weight roughly equal to 15 grams or half an ounce.</note> of each, and one lot of saltpeter. From these, distill a water. Then take six lots of mercury <gloss>mercurium</gloss>, put it into the water, and set it on sand for five hours; in this way the mercury will have transformed into a stone. Take an equal amount of calcined tartar <note>Potassium carbonate produced by heating the sediment found in wine barrels.</note> and two lots of eggshell lime <gloss>eijer kalch</gloss>, and one lot of silver litharge <note>original: "silber glet"; lead oxide, often a byproduct of silver refining, used here as a flux or pigment.</note> and eight lots of calcined sal ammoniac <unclear>salconi</unclear> <note>Likely ammonium chloride, a salt used to clean metal surfaces.</note> from the house. Grind all these powders together, finer and finer. And these powders should be steeped three times in oil of tartar <note>A concentrated solution of potassium carbonate, known for its caustic properties.</note>. And when they are ground together and mixed during the night and formed into lumps, then take <term>copper</term> <note>original: "venere"; the alchemical name for copper, associated with the planet Venus.</note> that has been well purified with glass and tartar, well refined together, and then quenched in <term>strong water</term> <note>original: "aqua fortz" (aqua fortis); nitric acid, used to etch or clean the metal.</note>—in this way it is well purified. Or take thin, hammered <gloss>hammered</gloss> pure smith's plate; heat it until it glows red hot and quench it three times in strong water. Then put the ingots <note>original: "lunken"; small cast blocks or bars of metal.</note> into a new pot or crucible; add one of the aforementioned lumps to it. Then place it in a <term>wind furnace</term> <note>original: "wind offen"; a high-heat furnace that uses a natural or bellows-driven draft.</note> for two hours. For the second stage, add two more lumps to it; seal the crucible very well and place it back in the wind furnace until it is burned off. This weight is for one mark <note>A unit of weight for precious metals, usually around 230-250 grams.</note>; therefore, divide the powder into these three lumps.

# How to make Copper white and pure <note>original: "Venus"; the alchemical name for copper.</note>

<margin>Also</margin> take four lots <note>A lot is a historical unit of weight, roughly 15 grams or half an ounce.</note> of white arsenic, two lots of mercury sublimate <note>original: "mercurium sublimatum"; a highly toxic compound of mercury and chlorine, used here to alter the metal's color.</note>, and one lot of burnt tartar <note>original: "winstein"; potassium carbonate produced by heating the sediment from wine barrels.</note>. Grind these together on a stone until they become a powder. Put the powder into parting water <note>original: "scheid wasser"; nitric acid, used to separate metals.</note> inside a glass vessel and let it stand overnight. In the morning, draw off the water using an alembic <note>A chemical still used for distillation.</note>; a white material will remain at the bottom. Take this out of the glass.
<margin><unclear>stir it once more</unclear></margin> And grind it again upon a stone and place it on the floor of a damp cellar. Leave it upon the stone and it will turn into water <note>This process, called deliquescence, involves the powder absorbing enough moisture from the humid cellar air to liquefy.</note>. Alternatively, hold the stone and make a hole in the hearth and place a glass beneath it, so that the water drips off the stone into the glass. Put this water into a glass or glazed vessel over the fire and let it become powder once again.

<margin>Also</margin> take three lots of this powder for every mark <note>A unit of weight for precious metals, roughly 230 grams.</note> of molten copper <gloss>venus</gloss> in a crucible. When it flows, stir it well with a small stick. This must be done with a good, hot fire. Then pour it out into an ingot mold <gloss>inguß</gloss> or into another vessel. Test the copper to see if you wish to use one lot for every three or four lots of silver; then you have a good work.

<margin>Also</margin> take as much copper as you wish and let it melt in a fire upon a refining sherd <note>A ceramic fragment used as a shallow crucible.</note> in a forge or a wind-furnace. Have ready beforehand one part glass, one part burnt tartar, and one part salt. Mix these together and throw the mixture often upon the copper <gloss>venus</gloss> while it is in flux. Stir it well through the metal. It will become as black as pitch; draw this [slag] off with an iron. The longer you continue throwing the powder, the better it becomes. This will then be good for making [the metal] white.

### But another whitening [recipe] from Nuremberg

Also take half a mark <note>A unit of weight for precious metals, roughly 230 grams.</note> of the prepared copper and let it melt well in a crucible. Add to it three lots <note>A lot is a historical unit of weight, roughly 15 grams or half an ounce.</note> of arsenic, piece by piece, one after another, while it is melting. Add to it also some burnt tartar <note>Potassium carbonate produced by heating the sediment from wine barrels.</note>—not too much, just a little at a time—and also pour in oil of tartar <note>original: "oleu tartaru"; a concentrated solution of potassium carbonate.</note>, which is tartar oil. Let these melt and flow well together, and afterwards pour it into urine, alum water, or honey. If there is slag <note>Dross or stony waste matter separated from metals during smelting.</note> attached to it when it is poured, knock the slag off with a small hammer. Make small pieces from the metal and let it melt once more. Add more sublimate <note>original: "sublimatz"; likely mercury sublimate, used to change the metal's color.</note>, also four lots in small pieces one after another, and let it all melt. Stir it well together in the crucible and then pour it again into alum water, granulated <note>original: "geküret"; the process of pouring molten metal through a broom or brush into water to create small beads or grains.</note> by pouring it through a broom. Then let it melt once more and pour it into oil of tartar or alum water, whichever you prefer. Then boil the copper in tartar and salt; thus it becomes a good whitening <note>original: "albu"; from the Latin 'albedo,' the alchemical stage of whitening.</note>.

Also take copper slag and boil it well with water or lye <note>original: "lög"</note> in a kettle and <term>pshūme</term> <note>The act of skimming the foam or impurities off the surface of a boiling liquid.</note> it well so that it becomes clean. Afterwards, boil it with alum water and let it become dry. Then place it in a shallow dish <note>original: "scherbe"; a ceramic shard or roasting dish used in assaying.</note> and purify it with glass, tartar, and salt when it melts, and proceed as was mentioned above regarding copper.

### To fix mercury

Also take one part of coagulated mercury <note>original: "merz coagulatũ"; mercury that has been thickened or solidified through previous chemical treatment.</note> and take one part glass-gall <note>original: "glasgall"; the dross or salty scum that forms on the surface of molten glass, often used as a flux in alchemical recipes.</note>. Grind or mix these well together and put them into an earthen vessel, well-closed and sealed with lute <note>original: "verlutiert"; an airtight clay or paste used to seal laboratory apparatus.</note>. Place it in a fire that has a gentle heat from below and above for eight hours. Then break open the vessel and examine it; if it is finished, then stop. But if it is not finished, put it back in and continue as before.

### But another way to fix

->mercury and other spirits<-

Also take nine lots <note>A historical unit of weight; one lot was approximately 15 grams.</note> or one pound of well-purified saltpeter, or one pound [total], and grind it well. Add this to the tartar <note>original: "tartarij"; potassium bitartrate, a byproduct of winemaking used frequently as a chemical reagent.</note> and it should be like a thick mush. After that, let it become dry. Also, then take a good new pot with a lid and make a gentle fire around it for one hour. After that, make the fire stronger until the material flows like an oil. Then let the material become cold. Also, after that, grind or crush it into a powder and put that same powder back into a paste with the tartar as before, using equal weight. Place it in another new pot with a lid and make it flow through the same process as before. Also, thus the material becomes just like an oil; it should be coagulated again into a powder and ground upon a stone.

Also, the material should afterwards be dissolved <note>original: "pluiere"; likely from the French *pluvier* or related to creating a liquid solution.</note> in a little warm water in a bowl. Immediately, the material dissolves into a liquid <note>original: "aq", abbreviation for *aqua* or water.</note> like a broth; with this, one fixes mercury. Also take this broth and put it in a glass flask <note>original: "colbe"; a long-necked distillation flask.</note> and put the mercury into it. Place an alembic <note>A helmet-like cap used in distillation to collect and direct vapors.</note> upon it and a glass [receiver] in front of it. Place it in a furnace with ash or sand and distill it as is customary. This should continue until two parts have distilled over and three parts remain at the bottom. Then let it cool and pour the liquid off from it; do this nine times.

# A ruby

Take two lots <note>A historical unit of weight; one lot was approximately 15 grams.</note> of sulfur, two lots of vitriol, and grind them small into a powder. After that, take copper and put it into a crucible *layer upon layer* <note>original: "stratu super stratu"; a method of alternating layers of different substances.</note> until the crucible is full. After that, close the top of the crucible with a lid <note>original: "termer"; a ceramic lid or cover.</note> so that the lid has a small hole in the very center, so that the moisture may escape. After that, set it upon a small stone and make a circle of fire around it so that the fire lies two spans away from the crucible for one hour. After that, bring the fire closer, more and more, until no more moisture is emitted at all. 

Then seal the crucible all around very well and let it glow for one or two hours, and yet the material must not melt <note>original: "fließe"; literally "flow," referring to the substance reaching its melting point.</note>. After that, let it cool, and whatever is brittle, crush that small. And take one and a half times as much <note>original: "drey halb"; likely meaning 1.5 parts relative to the mixture.</note> Venetian glass <term>Venetian glass: A high-quality, clear glass known for its purity, often used as the base for "pastes" or artificial gemstones.</term> and crush it also; then mix them together and put it into a crucible and melt it well together and let it flow well. 

And after it has cooled, it will settle as a "king" <note>original: "konig"; in alchemy, the "regulus" or the refined metallic button that settles at the bottom of a crucible after smelting.</note>. Take as much of that same "king" as is equal, crush it small, and let it melt. Pour it out onto a slab <note>original: "schlacht"; a casting plate or flat stone for cooling molten material.</note>, then take it off; keep that which is good for further use. And set it with coloring, which you make thus: 

Take one part *alazmear* <note>original: "alazmear"; likely an alchemical term for a mineral pigment or salt, possibly related to cinnabar or sal ammoniac.</note>, one part verdigris <term>verdigris: A green pigment (copper acetate) formed by the action of acetic acid on copper plates.</term>, one part saltpeter, one part vitriol, and crush them all small together and put them in a crucible and set it on a fire. Thus it will melt, and it will become like gold in appearance and beautiful.

<summary>This page provides a recipe for creating an artificial "ruby" or gold-like substance by heating copper with sulfur and vitriol, then fusing the resulting "king" (regulus) with Venetian glass and coloring agents.</summary>

->But an old [recipe]<-

Take <note>original: "Rp," the abbreviation for the Latin *Recipe*.</note> 4 lots <term>Lot: A historical German unit of weight, roughly 1/32 of a pound or about 15 grams.</term> of white arsenic <note>original: "arzē albū" (arsenicum album)</note> sublimated, 2 lots of saltpeter, 1 lot of rock salt <note>original: "salgeme" (sal gemmae)</note>, 1 lot of mercury sublimate <note>original: "mer. sublimaten" (mercurium sublimatum)</note>, and grind all of this together with one another. After that, take a small pot <term>Pot: The original "düppfi" is a diminutive, likely referring to a small crucible or ceramic vessel.</term> and a lid over it; seal it well with lute <note>original: "verlutierē"; sealing a vessel with a paste of clay or dung to make it airtight.</note>, and in the top of the lid make a small hole so that the smoke can escape. Keep the little hole open and set the pot in glowing coals; let it cook gently through and through until it no longer draws <note>Meaning it has finished off-gassing or smoking.</note>. And when it becomes cold, break the pot open and take the contents out; grind it well into a powder and <margin>M</margin> keep it. 

Afterwards, take 3 lots of Venus <note>Venus is the alchemical name for copper.</note> that has been calcined <note>original: "calcinieret"; reduced to a powder or oxide by heat.</note> with slag <note>original: "sinder stein"; dross or scale from a blacksmith's forge.</note> from the smithy and with Venetian glass. And then take those same 3 lots of Venus and melt it well. When it is well melted, then take the above-written powder, make 3 or 5 parts out of it, and throw it in 3 or 5 stages into the melted Venus. Each time, let it burn nicely until it has all flowed well in the crucible. Then take and pour it through a broom <note>A technique where molten metal is poured through twigs into water to create small, clean granules or "feathers."</note> and place it well into water so that it rings <note>original: "rincke"; likely referring to the metallic sound of the purified metal or the cleaning action of the water.</note> again. 

Then take it again and pour it again; and when it stands thus in flux, add as much good Moon <note>Moon (Luna) is the alchemical name for silver.</note> as there is Venus, and let it melt well together. Stir it well with a little stick, then take it out and pour it into an ingot mold <term>Ingot mold: The original "inguß" refers to a mold for casting metal bars or shapes.</term>. Then it is prepared. 

If, however, you want it to be malleable <note>original: "schmidig"; forgeable or soft enough to be worked by a hammer.</note> when the Moon and Venus are in flux: Take 3 quintins <term>Quintin: A small unit of weight, usually 1/4 of a lot.</term> of the powder as follows, and [add it] in 3 stages: Take 1 lot of white arsenic, 1 lot of borax <note>original: "borris".</note>, 1 lot of white frankincense <note>original: "wissen wirouch"</note>, 1 lot of saltpeter; and what was done with the above-written [process] should also be done with this.

<summary>This page outlines a recipe for a sublimated arsenic powder used to refine and alloy copper (Venus) and silver (Moon), including steps for sealing vessels with lute and ensuring the resulting metal is malleable.</summary>
<keywords>white arsenic, Venus (copper), Moon (silver), sublimation, calcination, crucible, ingot mold, borax, frankincense, metallurgy</keywords>

--- Page 234 ---
<meta>Continuity: This page marks a transition from the metallurgical and chemical recipes of the previous page toward veterinary medicine and folk remedies. The focus shifts from refining metals to treating ailments in livestock and humans, a common feature of medieval and early modern recipe books where "secrets" of all kinds were compiled together.</meta>

Also for the worm or the worms in a horse:
<margin>blossom</margin> take the blossom from the grain when it blooms; gather it and keep it for over a year. And when your horse has the worms <note>In this period, "the worm" could refer to internal parasites or various skin infections like farcy.</note>, take a little of the blossom and give it to the horse to eat in its fodder, or however you can give it to him, for eight days in a row; then it will be rid of the worms and healthy. This is frequently proven.

Also, if you want to cause a horse to have worms <note>This describes a malicious prank or folk-curse intended to make an animal appear diseased.</note>, then take lice from a sow or a piglet <note>original: "ferlin," a diminutive for a young pig.</note> and lay them on the horse; so worms will develop from them. And when you want to drive the worms away again, then do as is written above.

Also, if you want to drive away fig-warts <term>Fig-warts: Historically known as *ficus*, these were fleshy, wart-like growths, often associated with hemorrhoids or genital warts.</term>, then take a dove and roast it well and lay it then upon the warts; thus you will recover. And however often [you are afflicted], you will recover; this is also proven.

Also again for fig-warts in the private parts <note>original: "scham," referring to the genital or anal area.</note> or wherever they may be: take heron grease <term>Heron grease: The rendered fat of a heron, a common ingredient in medieval salves for its supposed ability to penetrate deep into the flesh.</term> and anoint yourself with it; then you will recover without a doubt.

<note>The terms "Head" and "Tail" of the Dragon refer to the Lunar Nodes—the points where the moon's orbit crosses the ecliptic. # Calendar Calculation Table

<note>This table is a tool for medieval timekeeping. The "Golden Number" (1 through 19) tracks the 19-year cycle of the moon, while the letters A through G are "Dominical Letters" assigned to days of the week. By finding the intersection of the current year's Golden Number and its Dominical Letter, a person could calculate specific liturgical dates or "hand-counts"—a mnemonic system where scholars used the joints of their fingers to keep track of complex calendar cycles.</note>

<meta>Following the visual diagrams of the hands on page 244, this page provides the introductory text for the study of chiromancy. It transitions from the graphical representation of the palm to a detailed explanation of its anatomy and the four principal lines used in medieval divination.</meta>

### 6

**Chiromancy** <note>The art of palm reading.</note> is an art by which one recognizes the natural character and the inclinations of people, as well as foreign habits, drunkenness, chastity, and unchastity, and others similar to these. And so that one might understand this art better, I will first explain the principles of the art. First, you should note that the part where the bone joins the hand is called the **wrist** <note>original German: *recept*, derived from the Latin *receptaculum*</note>. After that, toward the outer edge of the hand and the **pinky finger** <note>original: *ninsten vinger*, literally "the smallest finger"</note>, that is called the **table of the hand** <note>original: *tavell*; in palmistry, the *mensa* or "table" is the area between the two upper horizontal lines</note>. After that, the part from the wrist to the lower lines is called the **palm**. After that, the part between the fourth line and the finger is called the **bend of the finger**. After that, the hollow that is in the middle of the hand is called the **hollow** <note>original: *tocanū*, likely a scribal variant of the Latin *cavum* or "hollow of the hand"</note>. After that, where the first three lines close together, the part that lies in between is called the **triangle**.

Now you have the division of the hand. Next, I will speak of the main lines which appear in every person. The first begins between the first finger <note>the index finger</note> and the thumb and goes straight down toward the wrist; this is called the **Line of Life** <note>Latin: *linea vite*</note>. The second begins near the same place and goes toward the table of the hand; it is called the **Median Line** <note>Latin: *mediana*</note>. Now, the third begins near the wrist at the bottom and goes upward toward the second finger <note>the middle finger</note>; it is called the **Base of the Triangle** <note>original: *berion tanglū*, a likely corruption of the Latin *basis trianguli*</note>. The fourth begins under the pinky finger and stretches toward the first finger; it is called the **Table Line** <note>Latin: *mensalis*</note>. Now, the four lines that every person has have been described, though others do not have them all.

### The Natural Mean

**The Natural Mean** <term>Natural Mean: Latin *media naturalis*; in modern palmistry, this is known as the Head Line, reflecting the person's mental state, intellect, and temperament.</term>. When this line, which is called the **Natural Mean**, is of the correct width and the correct depth and a good color, that is a sign that the person is of a good nature, healthy, and of a good mind. It is also the case that if it is joined neatly, well-formed, and of a good color, that is a sign that the person is joyful. If it is large and wide in its path, that is a sign—that is a sign—that the person is of a foolish mind and is unchaste. But if it is crooked and bent, that signifies that the person is not steady in his words. If it is also small and has many pits in many places, that is a sign of an ungrateful and ignorant person. If this line is short...

### The Lower Triangle

The third line, which is called the **Lower Triangle** <term>Lower Triangle: Latin *inferior trianguli*; in historical chiromancy, this refers to the line forming the base of the "Great Triangle" of the palm, often associated with the Line of Health or the Liver Line.</term>, is not always found on every person. Since the life of a human is so noble and good, it is necessary that a person keeps themselves healthy. Thus, the greatest health for a person is to conduct themselves **temperately** <note>original: *messiclich*; referring to the medieval medical ideal of "moderation" in the non-naturals, such as diet and exercise</note> in eating and drinking at all times, both early and late, and furthermore by **letting their blood** <note>original: *lassende sein blut*; phlebotomy was a standard medical treatment used to balance the four humors</note> at the proper time.

Now one should know how one should let blood and at what times, and take note of what bloodletting is. As the **masters** <note>original: *maister*; likely referring to authoritative medical writers like Galen or Avicenna</note> write to us, bloodletting is a proper cutting open of the **veins** <note>original: *adern*; in medieval anatomy, the distinction between veins and arteries was understood differently than today</note> to observe the blood flowing out. For bloodletting is a beginning of health; it makes a person's thoughts clear, provides good senses, cleanses the **bladder** <note>original: *blateren*</note>, kills the burning <note>referring to inflammation or fever</note>, and cools the stomach. It strengthens the **marrow** <note>original: *marck*</note>, clears the ears, drives the **flux** <note>original: *flos*; a discharge of fluid or "rheum" thought to cause illness</note> from the eyes, cleanses the stomach, and drives [disease] from the skin of the person. It enables one to chew well, creates a clear voice, drives away sickness from the person, creates peaceful sleep, drives away **sluggishness** <note>original: *lasshait*</note> from the person, creates a good mood, drives away bad blood, and makes the person healthy and long-lived.

Furthermore, one should know that bloodletting is of two kinds:

The first is that you should let blood at the place where the **affliction** <note>original: *gesuchte*; a term often used for localized pain, swelling, or gout</note> arises, if it is that the affliction is increasing...

On the left side, you should let blood from the left arm. If the ailment is on the right side, then let it from the right arm.

¶ Furthermore, it is important to know that **elderly people** should by right sleep before they let blood, so that the blood may **gather** <unclear>ront</unclear> <note>original: *samny*; meaning to collect or settle</note>, and they should do so after eating; whereas the **young** should let blood before eating.

Yet one should know that many people should **bathe** on the day before they let blood so that the blood is **stirred together** <note>original: *zu sammen rure*; medieval medical theory suggested that bathing helped mobilize the humors, making the bloodletting more effective</note>. And **Master Galen** <note>original: *meister Galienus*; Galen of Pergamon (c. 129–216 AD), the Greek physician whose theories on the four humors dominated European medicine for over a millennium</note> says that whoever has a bad, **upset stomach** <note>original: *trunken magen*; literally "drunk stomach," referring to a stomach burdened by excess food or drink</note> should not let blood. And he forbids letting blood from the **cephalic vein** <note>original: *hohot ader*; literally the "head vein," located in the arm</note>, nor the **median vein** <note>original: *medianā*</note>, nor the **liver vein** <note>original: *leber [ader]*; the basilic vein, which medieval doctors believed was directly connected to the health of the liver</note>, nor the one on the elbow; furthermore, one should know that one must consider four kinds of things that are beneficial for bloodletting: the first is the **time**, the second is the **age**, the third is the **habit**, and the fourth is the **strength**.

Now, consider first the **time**, and that is indeed a great matter, for in the summer the weather is hot and people become weak. Now consider the **age** and know that no one should let blood who is **under twelve years old**. And certain people should not let blood when they become very old; however, **stout people** who have much blood should let it often so that they remain healthy. Now consider the **habit** and know that he who is not **accustomed** to the practice should not let blood.

# Properties of the Geomantic Figures

<note>Geomancy is a traditional method of divination based on patterns of dots. Each figure consists of four rows, with either one or two dots in each row. These figures are mapped to the "four humors" and astrological influences to provide a reading of a person's character or future.</note>
